extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational humor, computational linguistics, and AI (and informed general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, methods, and evaluation-relevant considerations for building and researching computational-humor systems (joke generation, recognition, and applications) in NLP/AI. Covers theoretical ingredients, algorithmic approaches, and example applications and evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of timing in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: An essentially new ingredient, a role of timing, is added to a well known role of ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is treated as a necessary ingredient in models of humorous effect; rapid deletion of a false interpretation (and the timing of that deletion) contributes to humor. Any computational model should represent and exploit timing/temporal dynamics in producing or modelling humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity/incongruity as core mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity (and incongruity theory) underlies humorous effects; classification and exploitation of ambiguity is central to analysis and generation of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems commonly use ambiguity/incongruity detection or generation (e.g., puns exploit lexical ambiguity). Approaches grounded in incongruity theory can be used for mnemonic generation and other applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for extensive databases for practical realization
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical realization of this algorithm needs extensive databases, whose creation in the automatic regime was suggested only recently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of large, structured lexical/semantic/pragmatic datasets has hampered development; effective systems often require substantial curated resources (lexicons, templates, mappings) or large corpora for statistical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify jokes as basis for generation
rubrics_metrics.description: An approach to analysis of humor is classification of jokes. A further step is an attempt to generate jokes basing on the rules that underlie classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should identify joke types (puns, knock-knock, question-answer, acronyms) and codify generation rules tailored to each class rather than a one-size-fits-all generator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based pun generation from non-humorous lexicons
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple prototypes for computer pun generation were reported in the early 1990s, based on a natural language generator program, VINCI; JAPE was designed to generate question-answer-type puns from a general, i.e., non-humorous, lexicon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-based templates and mappings from lexicon entries to joke templates (e.g., question-answer) are viable; examples (JAPE) show concrete outputs and serve as a modeling pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-answer pun generation (JAPE/STANDUP examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: JAPE produced question-answer-type puns (e.g., 'What do you call a strange market? A bizarre bazaar'). STANDUP is a later generator implemented in Java.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems can target specific formats like Q&A puns and evaluate using generated examples and human reaction; STANDUP was evaluated with child users to measure usability and language-learning benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application for language acquisition and therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: A possible application for assistance in language acquisition is described; STANDUP was tested on children, including those with communication disabilities, showing enthusiasm and marked improvement on certain language tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the goal is pedagogical or therapeutic, evaluation metrics include user engagement, measurable language-skill improvements, and usability for target populations rather than purely 'funniness' scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-case tradeoff: quantity vs quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Another envisioned use of joke generators is in cases of a steady supply of jokes where quantity is more important than quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define application requirements: some deployments prioritize throughput (many acceptable jokes) while others prioritize high-quality humorous output; system design and evaluation metrics should match that tradeoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated joke appreciation as a research direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Another obvious, yet remote, direction is automated joke appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond generation and recognition, modeling appreciation (evaluating funniness, timing, social appropriateness) is an advanced goal requiring models of audience response and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of humor in human–computer interaction (HCI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans interact with computers in ways similar to interacting with other humans described in terms of personality, politeness, flattery, and in-group favoritism; therefore, the role of humor in human–computer interaction is being investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In HCI applications humor should be used to ease communication, convey personality, and fit social norms; evaluation should consider user perception of personality, politeness, and appropriateness as well as task performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: MnemonicSentence approach: using incongruity to aid memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Craig McDonough implemented the Mnemonic Sentence Generator, which converts passwords into humorous sentences based on the incongruity theory of humor to make them easier to remember.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications can leverage humor's mnemonic effect; evaluation should measure memorability and error rates in recall compared to non-humorous methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical ML for double-entendre detection (TWSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statistical machine learning algorithm to detect whether a sentence contained a 'That's what she said' double entendre was developed by Kiddon and Brun (2011).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition tasks can be framed as supervised classification problems; open-source implementations (e.g., TWSS Python project) enable reproduction and benchmarking on annotated corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine learning to distinguish jokes from non-jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: An application of machine learning techniques for distinguishing joke texts from non-jokes was described by Mihalcea and Strapparava (2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature engineering and corpus labeling are key; evaluation is typical ML metrics (accuracy, precision/recall) on held-out datasets, and robustness across genres should be tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic programs for pun detection in other languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Takizawa et al. (1996) reported on a heuristic program for detecting puns in the Japanese language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language-specific phonological, morphological, and orthographic properties require tailored heuristics or models; cross-lingual transfer is nontrivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing structured joke formats (e.g., knock-knock)
rubrics_metrics.description: A program to recognize knock-knock jokes was reported by Taylor and Mazlack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured joke formats can be detected by modeling dialog patterns and fixed templates; recognition supports downstream tasks like classification or response generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating humorous acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock and Strapparava described a program to generate funny acronyms (HAHAcronym).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acronym generation combines lexical selection with constraints on pronounceability and humorous associations; evaluation includes human judgments of funniness and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational systems leveraging humor for human-likeness (Turing test relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversational systems designed for Turing test competitions generally have the ability to learn humorous anecdotes and jokes; humor can be useful in convincing a human interrogator that a hidden entity is human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To pass as human, conversational agents should learn, time, and deploy humor appropriately; evaluation may include Turing-style human judgments and crowd-sourced realism scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical/formal models of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: John Allen Paulos demonstrates structures common to humor and formal sciences and develops a mathematical model of jokes based on catastrophe theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalizing humor (e.g., via mathematical models) can clarify structural properties; such models suggest formal constraints or invariants useful for generative or evaluative systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural-network model of humor and laughter mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Suslov suggested a computational model where deletion of a false version corresponds to zeroing part of the neural network and excessive neuronal energy is thrown out to the motor cortex, arousing muscular contractions (laughter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cognitive/neural-inspired models link internal representational dynamics (e.g., belief updating, suppression) to observable responses like laughter; they motivate architectures that model false-hypothesis generation and rapid revision.
